guide: V35 labeling guide + V36 addendum (adversarial categories); each author saw only a catalog of grounded source sentences
note: V36 development split: three independent annotators (C, D, E), seven documents, Mobile Mastery at most 40%. Used to calibrate V36 semantic thresholds; never a sealed set.

cases.text: Think in a news app. You open it and yesterday's headlines appear on the moment; while you read, in the background it fetches the new ones and swaps them. Price: for a while you may see old news. Gain: you kill two rabbits with one blow - it is quick, and it still shows something when the server is sick.
credits: Serve slightly stale cached data immediately
trades bounded freshness for low latency
cases.notes: The news-app scenario shows the old copy served at once, the refresh in the background, and the trade of brief staleness for speed and resilience, with nothing wrong.
cases.author: C

cases.text: You take the sorted list and look to the element in the middle. If your target is bigger, the whole left half you can forget; if it is smaller, the right half. Then the same thing with the half that stayed, again and again, until you find it or nothing is left to look.
credits: repeatedly narrows a sorted search space
cases.notes: Repeatedly discarding the half of a sorted list that cannot hold the target is exactly the source's mechanism, in the learner's own words.
cases.author: C

cases.text: Binary search works on a sorted array: every step it cuts the zone where it searches in two and continues only in one piece, untill it finds the value. It is so fast because it uses the binary representation of the numbers, the zeros and ones, which is the natural language of the processor.
credits: repeatedly narrows a sorted search space
cases.notes: The mechanism (repeatedly narrowing a sorted array) is right, but the reason offered for its speed is a 'binary means bits' non-sequitur that the source does not support.

cases.text: The arrow function that counter() gives back carries the value variable with it, like a backpack. counter() is already finished, but next() still reaches that same variable and adds to it: 1, then 2. And each new call of counter() packs a new backpack, so two counters never mix their numbers.
credits: keep accessing that environment after the outer
create two independent environments
cases.notes: Through the counter example and a backpack analogy it shows that access survives the outer call and that each call gets its own environment; the general definition is only implied, so that sentence is not credited.

cases.text: comp root = the spot at startup (main(), app bootstrap) where you actually new up the real impls and inject them. everything downstream codes against interfaces and never picks an impl itself. think Spring ApplicationContext / Guice module / wire.Build in Go.

cases.notes: Startup wiring creates the real implementations and injects them into interface-only consumers, which is the source's single sentence in DI jargon.

cases.text: root of the app wires the graph: for each interface it picks the concrete class + passes it in. callers just take what they're handed (Dagger component / fx.Provide, same idea).

cases.author: D

cases.text: ok so in any DI setup you've got interfaces all over the place, and at some point somebody has to decide 'this Cache is Redis in prod, a plain map in tests'. that somebody is main.go (or Program.cs / the startup class if you're in .NET land). it builds the whole object graph and feeds each consumer its real dep. the consumers get zero say in which impl they end up with, they just take the interface they asked for.
credits: supplies the concrete implementation
cases.notes: Long and chatty but fully right: the startup code decides and hands each consumer its concrete implementation, and consumers don't choose.

cases.text: It's when you split things out into seperate tables so each value lives in exactly one place -> zero dupes. Tradeoff: lookups get slower (more joins), inserts/updates + disk get cheaper.

cases.text: Conditional types = if/else at the type level: `T extends U ? X : Y`, where extends means 'is assignable to', not strict equality. You reach for them in generic code to transform one type into another — unwrap a Promise, pull the id type off an entity w/ infer, filter members out of a union. ts-toolbelt / type-fest are basically built on them. And unlike Java's erased generics these actually get evaluated at runtime, so a bad payload gets rejected before it hits your handler.

misconceptions.claim: type-level if/else based on assignability

credits: enables expressive generic transformations
cases.notes: All correct until the closing claim that they are evaluated at runtime, which contradicts their type-level nature; the definition sentence is not credited because that clause undercuts it.
cases.author: D

cases.text: Deep copy walks the whole tree and clones every nested obj/array, so the copy shares no refs with the original — mutate the clone all you want, source is untouched. structuredClone does it natively now, or lodash cloneDeep. Downside: it's expensive on big graphs, and blindly cloning stuff like class instances w/ methods, DOM nodes or anything w/ identity semantics is just wrong. For plain state updates though, `{...state}` already gives you a deep copy, so you rarely need the heavy tools.

misconceptions.claim: instead of sharing the same nested object

credits: full cloning can be costly or semantically
cases.notes: Definition and the cost/special-object caveat are right, but calling `{...state}` a deep copy confuses it with a shallow copy whose nested references are still shared, so the definition is not credited.
cases.author: D

cases.text: keyof T -> union of T's prop names as string literal types, e.g. keyof {id: number; name: string} = 'id' | 'name'. point: `get<K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K)` means a caller can't pass a key that doesn't exist — compile error, not undefined at runtime. (don't mix it up w/ typeof, which lifts a value's type into type space.)
credits: produces a union of the property names
lets APIs accept only valid keys
cases.notes: Union of property names and the purpose (callers can only pass real keys) are both right, and the typeof aside is accurate.
